newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Italian rally has further to run.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Italian rally has further to run.

text.p: Italian bonds have been carried skyward on a wave of optimism about the country's potential to slash its deficit and qualify for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), analysts said on Thursday.
And while a disappointing 1997 budget could bring the rally to a screeching halt, the Italian market can outperform core European bonds and its Spanish cousin longer term, they said.
"If we see a (budget) package that falls short of expectations the market is exposed to profit-taking," said Lorenzo Codogno, head of economics at Bank of America in Milan.
"But I think overall it will be convincing," he said.
Italian bonds have taken off this week as EMU convergence trades sprang back into vogue after European Union finance ministers meeting in Dublin last weekend gave EMU a big boost.
Italian debt futures listed in London soared past their all-time high of 119.15 set in February 1994 to hurtle more than three full points in a week to a new record at 120.98.
The cash market has soared too as some market players even began to talk about Italy joining EMU in the 1999 first round.
The BTP/Bund 10-year yield spread has shrunk in a week from 300 basis points to its narrowest point in a year at 266.
Such a stellar performance has made the market vulnerable to profit-taking and investors could find no better excuse than the 1997 budget, expected on Friday, analysts said.

The government has hinted it will try to cut the 1997 deficit by more than 32.4 trillion lire. Italian newspapers reported on Thursday the government was considering a figure of 38.5 trillion lire, plus a "tax for Europe" that would raise an additional 22 trillion lire in the coming months.
But the hard-left Communist Refoundation Party has vowed to fight the government every step of the way if they try to cut spending on health and pensions.

Codogno said key for debt markets was whether the government's spending cuts were credible. He said small revenue raising measures like the sale of government real estate or tougher tax evasion rules were unlikely to produce significant windfalls and would not wash with the markets.
The government would have a better chance making real cuts in the deficit by focusing on tax raising instead, he said.
Phyllis Reed, European bond strategist at BZW in London, said a disappointing budget could see the BTP/Bund gap snap back to 300 quite quickly.

Beyond the budget, however, the market could gain, she said. Reed targets the BTP/Bund gap at 250 basis point by the end of 1997, as interest rate cuts begin to come through. She expects to see 50 basis points off the 8.25 percent discount rate before the end of the year and a full percentage point in 1997.
"The short-end of the curve is still quite clearly good value," said Reed, forecasting the yield on three-month bills at 6.75 percent by the end of 1997 from the current 8.07 percent.
Reed, and Ernesto Rameriez, European economist at Bankers Trust in London, would both choose Italian bonds over Spanish.
"Inflation in Italy is going to be better than Spain and monetary easing is going to be much larger," Rameriez said.
Rameriez has a 225 basis point target for the BTP/Bund gap by the end of 1997 but Codogno and Reed would not go so far.
The idea of Italy joining EMU at the 1999 start date was too optimistic for now, said Reed.

"To cut our target any further I think we have to really start to feel comfortable with factoring in some EMU pariticipation and this is something we don't really think is possible at this stage of the game," she said.

Even with a special EMU tax the 1997 budget would still leave Italy well short of the three percent deficit-to-GDP ratio needed by end-1997 to qualify in 1999, analysts said. Current government forecasts predict a deficit/GDP ratio of 4.52 percent next year and 2.99 percent in 1998.
